title: Why Did Patisserie Valerie Collapse? The Secret Overdrafts
summary:
Patisserie Valerie collapse explained from company, regulator and Serious Fraud Office records.
Worth £450m on a Tuesday in October 2018, shares frozen by Wednesday. Using Patisserie Holdings' own stock-market announcements, the Financial Reporting Council's sanctions against its auditor Grant Thornton, and the SFO's case file, we separate what the company disclosed, what the regulator found, and what is still only alleged, as the fraud trial moves to January 2028.

scenes.say: On a Tuesday in October 2018, Patisserie Valerie's owner was worth about four hundred and fifty million pounds. By Wednesday afternoon, its shares were frozen.

visual.label: stock-market value of Patisserie Holdings, 9 Oct 2018

scenes.say: The company said it had been notified of significant, and potentially fraudulent, accounting irregularities.

visual.text: significant, and potentially fraudulent, accounting irregularities

scenes.say: Within days, its chairman said he hadn't even known the company had bank overdrafts. There were two of them, worth almost ten million pounds.
Eight years on, nobody has been convicted of anything. The criminal trial has just been pushed back to 2028.

visual.src: SFO case page: Patisserie Holdings plc

scenes.src: SFO case page: Patisserie Holdings plc

scenes.say: So what does the official record actually establish? And who saw the warning signs, years earlier, and missed them? Hold on to that second question.
We go through the paperwork: the company's own stock-market announcements, the audit regulator's sanctions, and the Serious Fraud Office's case file.

visual.title: The paperwork
items: Serious Fraud Office charges and court listings, 2023 to 2026

scenes.say: Chapter 1. A cake shop from 1926.
The story starts in 1926, on Frith Street in Soho, with a Belgian woman remembered only as Madame Valerie.

visual.text: First shop opens on Frith Street, Soho

scenes.say: The first café was bombed during the Second World War. In the 1940s it moved around the corner to Old Compton Street, and stayed there for about seventy years.

visual.title: Old Compton Street
lines: Original café bombed in the Second World War

scenes.say: By 2018 the brand had grown into a listed company, Patisserie Holdings, with almost two hundred high-street bakeries.
On paper it was a rare thing: a cake chain the stock market adored. On the ninth of October 2018 its shares closed at four hundred and twenty-nine and a half pence.
The man in the chair was Luke Johnson, the executive chairman and largest shareholder. The finance director was Chris Marsh.
Keep that word cash in mind. Everything in this story turns on how much of it the company really had.
Chapter 2. Wednesday, 10 October 2018.
On Wednesday the tenth of October 2018, Patisserie Holdings told the market it had been notified of significant, and potentially fraudulent, accounting irregularities.
It said the irregularities had significantly impacted its cash position, and might lead to a material change in its overall financial position.

visual.text: significantly impacted the company's cash position and may lead to a material change in its overall financial position

scenes.say: It asked for its shares to be suspended, and said its finance chief, Chris Marsh, had been suspended too.
Its shares traded on AIM, the London Stock Exchange's market for smaller growing companies. A suspension means nobody can buy or sell them. Investors were locked in.
There was a second disclosure that day. The taxman had filed a winding-up petition against the main trading company, Stonebeach, over one point one four million pounds.
A company valued at four hundred and fifty million pounds, facing a court petition over one point one million pounds of tax. That doesn't add up, and it was the first public crack.
Luke Johnson said: we are all deeply concerned about this news and the potential impact on the business.

visual.text: We are all deeply concerned about this news and the potential impact on the business.

scenes.say: Two days later, the Serious Fraud Office opened a criminal investigation. Its codename was Operation Venom.
By the following week, the trade press reported that the finance director had been arrested and bailed. Being arrested is not a finding of guilt.

visual.sub: No one has been convicted in this case.

scenes.say: Chapter 3. The overdrafts nobody knew about.
On the twelfth of October the company published a rescue plan. It began with a remarkable admission.
Its words: historical statements on the cash position of the Company were mis-stated.

visual.text: Historical statements on the cash position of the Company were mis-stated

scenes.say: Instead of cash in the bank, the board now estimated net debt of about nine point eight million pounds.
It said it needed an immediate cash injection of no less than twenty million pounds. Without it, there was no scope for the group to continue trading in its current form.

visual.text: no scope for the Group to continue trading in its current form

scenes.say: The money came from two places. Luke Johnson offered a ten million pound loan for three years, interest free and fee free, plus a bridging loan of up to ten million more.
And new shares were to be placed at fifty pence each, to raise about fifteen million pounds. Three days earlier, the shares had been worth more than eight times that.
Put simply, anyone who bought at the old price had lost almost nine tenths of it, on paper, before the full picture was even known.
Then the story got stranger. The company found two overdrafts, at HSBC and Barclays, that had been set up without the board's knowledge.
Nine point seven million pounds had been drawn on them.

visual.label: drawn on overdrafts the board didn't know about

scenes.say: Johnson told The Sunday Times: I didn't even know there were bank overdraft facilities. He called the week a nightmare.

visual.text: I didn't even know there were bank overdraft facilities.
visual.by: Luke Johnson to The Sunday Times, Oct 2018

scenes.say: He added that the banks were as shocked as the board, and, he was sure, the auditors. Remember the auditors. We'll come back to them.

visual.text: the banks were as shocked by things as we, the board were, as I'm sure are the auditors

scenes.say: Chapter 4. The end of the counter.
The rescue bought three months. In January 2019 the company could not renew its banking facilities with HSBC and Barclays.
It entered administration, with KPMG appointed as administrator. The company blamed what it called the significant fraud.

visual.text: As a direct result of the significant fraud referred to in previous announcements

scenes.say: The first wave of closures took in twenty-seven Patisserie Valerie shops, nineteen Druckers cafés, twenty-five concessions, and the Spitalfields bakery.
Nine hundred and twenty people were made redundant.
On the twenty-third of January 2019, the shop on Old Compton Street, home to the brand for about seventy years, closed its doors.
Johnson made a further interest-free loan, so staff in the surviving business could be paid their January wages.
One hundred and twenty-two outlets kept trading while the administrators looked for a buyer. Mike Ashley's Sports Direct bid, then withdrew, complaining it had been locked out of the process.
In February, the Dublin-based investor Causeway Capital Partners bought ninety-six Patisserie Valerie sites, saving nearly two thousand jobs.
The brand survived. The listed company, and its shareholders' four hundred and fifty million pound valuation, did not.

visual.text: The cakes survived. The company didn't.

scenes.say: Chapter 5. Where were the auditors?.
Now, that second question. The company's auditor since 2007 was Grant Thornton, and it signed clean audit opinions for 2015, 2016 and 2017.
In September 2021 the audit regulator, the Financial Reporting Council, published its sanctions. Grant Thornton and its audit partner, David Newstead, had admitted failures.
The admitted failures covered four areas: revenue, cash, journals, and additions to fixed assets. They happened in every one of the three years.
The FRC said they reflected lapses in professional judgement, professional scepticism, audit evidence and documentation.
The regulator's deputy executive counsel, Claudia Mortimore, said the case showed a serious lack of competence in conducting the audit work.

visual.text: a serious lack of competence in conducting the audit work

scenes.say: She listed missed red flags, a failure to obtain enough audit evidence, and a failure to stand back and question what management provided.

visual.text: a failure to stand back and question information provided by management

scenes.say: Press reports of the decision gave examples. Third-party invoices were accepted despite missing branding, typing errors and wrong addresses.

visual.title: Invoices accepted
visual.src: Yahoo News report of FRC notice, Sep 2021

scenes.src: Yahoo News report of FRC notice, Sep 2021

scenes.say: And in 2016, three quarters of the year's voucher income was reportedly paid in a single transaction. The auditors didn't ask about it.

visual.label: of 2016 voucher income in one transaction, as reported
visual.src: Yahoo News report of FRC notice, Sep 2021

scenes.src: Yahoo News report of FRC notice, Sep 2021

scenes.say: The fines. Grant Thornton's starting sanction was four million pounds, cut to two point three four million after discounts for admissions and cooperation.
David Newstead's fine fell from one hundred and fifty thousand pounds to eighty-seven thousand, seven hundred and fifty, with a three-year ban on signing audits.
Both received a severe reprimand, and a declaration that each audit report failed to meet the required standards.

visual.title: Declaration
lines: !Audit reports did not meet the Relevant Requirements

scenes.say: The FRC also ordered Grant Thornton to report to it every year for three years on its fixes, review its culture of challenge, and accept extra monitoring of its bank and cash audit work.

visual.title: Non-financial sanctions
items: Annual reports to the FRC for three years
Review of the firm's culture of challenge
Extra monitoring of bank and cash audit work

scenes.say: There was a civil case too. The administrators sought around two hundred million pounds from Grant Thornton. In 2022 it was settled for an undisclosed multi-million pound sum.
Luke Johnson, who is not accused of any wrongdoing, was among the largest creditors. He has said other executive directors misled him with a false picture of the finances, Consultancy.uk reported.

visual.title: The chairman's account
lines: !Says he was given a false picture of the finances

scenes.say: Chapter 6. The criminal case.
Back to the Serious Fraud Office. In June 2019, five more people were arrested and interviewed, in a joint operation with three police forces.
Then, nearly five years after the collapse, in September 2023, the SFO charged four people.

visual.src: SFO case page: Patisserie Holdings plc

scenes.src: SFO case page: Patisserie Holdings plc

scenes.say: They are Christopher Marsh, the former finance director; Louise Marsh, an accountant and his wife; Pritesh Mistry, the financial controller; and Nileshkumar Lad, a financial consultant.

visual.title: Charged, September 2023
visual.src: SFO case page: Patisserie Holdings plc

scenes.src: SFO case page: Patisserie Holdings plc

scenes.say: The SFO's director at the time, Lisa Osofsky, said the collapse rocked our high streets, leaving boarded-up shops and devastating job losses.

visual.text: Patisserie Valerie's abrupt collapse rocked our high streets – leaving boarded-up shops, devastating job losses

scenes.say: The SFO alleges they conspired to inflate the cash in the company's balance sheets and annual reports from 2015 to 2018, including by giving false documents to the auditors.

The SFO says the company reported twenty-eight million pounds in its accounts, while ten million pounds of debt was hidden from investors and creditors. That is the prosecution's case, and it is untested in court.
On the twenty-sixth of April 2024, at Southwark Crown Court, all four pleaded not guilty to all charges.

visual.src: SFO case page: Patisserie Holdings plc

scenes.src: SFO case page: Patisserie Holdings plc

scenes.say: The trial was listed for March 2026. Then, on the ninth of February 2026, it was relisted for the fourth of January 2028.

visual.title: Trial date
visual.src: SFO case page: Patisserie Holdings plc

scenes.src: SFO case page: Patisserie Holdings plc

scenes.say: The published listings give no reason for the delay. By then, it will be more than nine years since the investigation began.

So, to be precise: the irregularities and the hidden overdrafts were the company's own disclosures. The audit failings are the regulator's findings. The fraud charges are allegations, and all four deny them.

visual.title: What kind of fact is it?
items: Company disclosure: irregularities, mis-stated cash, overdrafts
Allegation only: the fraud charges, denied

scenes.say: Chapter 7. Our analysis.
Here's what we think the paperwork shows. First: cash is supposed to be the hardest number to fake.

visual.text: Cash is the hardest number to fake.

scenes.say: Profits involve judgement. A bank balance should be one phone call to the bank away. Yet the company itself admitted its historical cash statements were wrong.

visual.text: Historical statements on the cash position of the Company were mis-stated

scenes.say: Second: the warning signs weren't hidden in some vault. The regulator found missed red flags across three separate audit years, and the firm admitted it.

Third: the first to pay were staff and shareholders. Nine hundred and twenty staff were made redundant as administration began. Shareholders saw a four hundred and fifty million pound valuation wiped out.
Fourth: justice is slow. Irregularities disclosed in 2018 will not reach a jury until 2028, and until then, four people remain innocent in law.

visual.src: SFO case page: Patisserie Holdings plc

scenes.src: SFO case page: Patisserie Holdings plc

scenes.say: And the comeback? By September 2023, Time Out reported the chain was down to twenty-nine cafés from a peak of one hundred and ninety-three, and was reopening some sites.

The new owner inherited a mess. Time Out reported broken ovens left unused for months, unpaid suppliers, and a leaking roof at head office. At one point, money was so short the chain stopped using butter in its puff pastry.
Its cakes are still sold in around four hundred Sainsbury's supermarkets. The name outlived the company that owned it.
Patisserie Valerie wasn't killed by bad cakes. According to the company's own disclosures, it was killed by numbers that weren't true.
